I reported on a small female with these conditions last year, and this could be her again. The paws were closed across the chest, so couldn't see gland markings. I rang Redlands Wildlife Ambulance immediately, but when they arrived, the koala had moved. We all searched the area, but couldn't find her. I found fresh urine and Megan found the small, pale green scats next to the urine. The urine had the distinctive odour of cystitis. I used to smell it all the time when the little female was around last year. Ambos tried twice last year to catch her then, but she bolted for the canopy each time.

Delighted to actually hear him after all year with only 1 record. The numbers of calls in one go was over 20, so wondered if it was  Pavarotti  from last breeding season. Pav usually calls up to 60 times in the one session. This male made no noise in the inhale, only the usual exhale noise, but he was gripunting away for over 20 times after I started counting

This is the FIRST  ( and only) Koala we have EVER seen on our 40 acres. We have lived here 20 years now. Rural acreage mostly cleared already with some patches lightly forested.  Surrounded by other rural blocks ( mostly cleared). We are near Mt Neurum and D’Aguilar National Park. Koala was seen MOVING on GROUND ( for 40 metres) and then went up ( ?Grey Gum ) tree . Still asleep there this afternoon.  The only other Koala we have seen in the area is one we rescued, injured on road near Stanley River, towards Woodford. Seen  3 echidnas ( >10 years ago) . Have wallabies, mountain possums, squirrel gliders, phascogales, bandicoots, few water dragons, one frilled neck lizard, few goannas, few pythons, few red-bellied blacks, few brown snakes, plenty geckos, green tree fogs ( and others reported on Frog ID), plenty tree snakes, parrots = king, Rainbow l., yellow-headed, scaly br, galahs. Channel- billed c., little grebes, 3  occasional dingoes ( and foxes), 2 brush turkeys.  and more ! Would like to record more in future. I have degree in Zoology. Unfortunately I worked in healthcare ( by default!)

records.locality: Wildflower Garden, Black Hill Conservation Park. This koala came up Addison Ave, and entered the park. It sat in the shade near the building, and accepted several drinks of water.
records.notes: The koala came up Addison Ave, outside the park, along the footpath, and game in through the gate.  I headed along the path towards a shady area near the building. It stopped when it noticed me, and watched me for a while.  It checked a couple of trees (planted melaleucas) and I thought it had climbed one, but shortly after, I noticed it had returned to the ground, and was lying spread out somewhat on a rock on the ground.  I offered it water and it drank.  Returning the next day, it was still in the same location. I offered it water again, and it drank. An hour later I offered more water and it drank again.  Each time, I offered it only a small amount of water from a running hose, leaving it run for maybe 2 minutes as it lapped it up. The third day the weather was cooler over night, and it was no-where to be seen, a small pile of droppings (they were not remarkable) were left, near where it had been. It was a mature male, with the gland markings on the chest. It appeared to be in good condition, apart from its unusual behaviour.

This Koala is going to pop up on a lot of facebook feeds. It was strolling along the roadside on the Great Ocean Road during the marathon. Hubby (and a lot of other runners I believe) snapped photos as they ran by. Apparently the Koala was unperturbed by the multitude of humans fleeing from an imaginary foe. (There must have been something chasing them or else why were they running?????) When comparing 'notes' later my son who ran the half marathon said that he spotted about 5 Koalas in trees roadside in the same stretch of road. The koala obviously waited till the human congestion died down before crossing the road.

My brother, his friend heard this weird noise (I'm not sure how to describe it) and saw an adult koala trying to climb up a tree that another koala was already in. The koala above the intruder started to climb down the tree and continued to make the weird noise until the intruder lumbered off to another tree. My brother, his friend and I walked a little closer to the tree and when looking through the branches, I saw a young koala. I was so excited, it was the cutest thing in the world. I'm assuming that the (female?) koala was protecting its baby and tree from the other koala, who was probably a male. When walking down the hill, I spotted another adult koala resting. Once again, the location may not be 100% accurate.

Had to shoo 'Old Boy' off the road, he didn't want to move. Kim Hunter, wildlife carer extraordinaire, came (with 5 wallabies) to move him somewhere safer. He had been hit by a car in the past and was returning to the bush from 'Wild Haven'. While I was waiting for Kim I heard another in a tree nearby: Kim tells me that must be Jamie. If I saw how Kim handled him and his claws and teeth, I would have been far more scared shooing him off the road with a cushion from my car!

Appearance: Medium-sized marsupial, grayish-brown fur with lighter patches. Large, fluffy ears.Behavior: Solitary and arboreal; observed climbing and resting in eucalyptus trees.Feeding: Strictly herbivorous, specialising in eucalyptus leaves.Vocalizations: Occasional grunts and bellows during mating season; otherwise quiet.Habitat: Prefers mature eucalyptus forests from coast to mountains.Reproduction: Breeding season from August to February; females rear single young in pouch.Conservation: Faces threats from habitat loss, road accidents, and disease; crucial to local ecosystem health.Conclusion: The Queensland Koala adapts well to diverse habitats within Queensland, playing a vital ecological role despite conservation challenges.

There are a lot of these around now that the bushfire has burnt the conservation park
Not a Koala bear or a mammal. Its a marsupial. Observed chilling out on a bottle brush tree in our back yard and was not fussed of us.
Not the best image but unmistakable what it is. Sitting high in an unknown species of Eucalyptus, not surprisingly given it spends much of the day eating the leaves of these trees.

Fat and healthy looking specimen. Living in  a small bushland reserve (dry eucalypt forest) next to a power station, close to a busy road. Alert and interactive in the daytime. No evidence of babies or other relatives in the reserve (quite rare to spot this animal so close to town).
An unfortunate find in our front yard: the forelimb of a mammal.Notable features include obvious fingerprints and the two fingers closest to the thumb are fused, apart from the claws.
Spotted at Anstey Hill, during my morning walk
Always in the valley at Morialta.
gorgeous visitor to our camp-site. we think a female as the belly looked very heavy when it walked.
Grey-brown arboreal marsupial. Large fluffy white ears. Sleeps most of the time and eats gum leaves the rest of the time.
This big fella was just climbing the tree but stopped to snack on the little branch right in front of him. He needs to keep eating. And sleeping.

This guy was just chilling in the tree. Neither sleeping or eating, which is a bit unusual, and looked like it was missing only a cocktail or a G&T perhaps. Then it noticed me, and I apologised for disturbing it and kept walking. Australian wildlife is the best.

Cute little fella! I think this specimen must  recently left mum. It is the smallest one I've  seen. Grey and brown fur all over but a streak of white across the chest. Looked a little miserable in the rain.

Sighted in mountainous bushland reserve on the edge of town. Despite it being mid-morning, this smallish cuddly bear was not only awake but very active. In the five minutes we observed her she munched some tasty gum leaves, craned around to look for better pickings then jumped (yes! I couldn’t believe it!) three times to make her way towards a slender upper branch where she showed no concern whatsoever at being swayed to dubious angles by the the gusting autumn wind. You may gather by my description that I was completely pumped by the experience (my previous sightings of these animals in the wild have been so still you’d swear they were stuffed!)
A cute grey mammal up a gum tree.
He claimed on to the second story of our house and sat on this pole all day he is safely back home in a gum tree now though

(-27.5103444, 153.0855369) observed at 10:13am 04/07/21 a sunny day after several days rain 1x female + 1x juvenile  and a separate sex-undetermined individual all sleeping and all visible in tree tops 6-15m from the Ridge Line track at Whites Hill Bushland Reserve.
First time we have seen one in Carrington Rd
Relaxing approximately 15m from the ground in an Angophora costata tree. We see them here from time to time, but never when we look for them.
a young koala taking his/her morning stroll at the Qld/NSW border
Not a very good photo (sorry). A mammal that sits in the tree eating leaves and sleeping all day. Made a very distinct grunting noise
Grey iconic Australian marsupial spotted up a gum tree
Large, arboreal mammal taking a nap. Poor thing was being harassed by currawongs
A lot like a koala but hangs from the underside of the branch. Was too scared to walk underneath in case it dropped on me. Was making a horrible squeaking sound
Iconic grey Australian mammal halfway up a gum tree.
Two animals resting in tree during heat of day.
Captured on remote motion-activated infrared camera in an intact old growth bushland remnant. There has been an increasing amount of night time roaring as spring progresses.
Two adults in a gum. One with a baby on its back!
Observed sleeping, and then waking up to scratch itself, yawn, and start calling. Was not as large as others in the area, may just have been matured.
Located in bush regeneration area, cleared in 1995 with only isolated mature trees left. Thick scrub has regenerated, however there is still quite a walk between large trees in some areas.
Found in a tree just above head height with a baby on its back.
In suburban backyard. Across from parkland. Regularly seen in warmer months looking for food and water
Koala seen in a area where there had been fire
Iconic Australian mammal up gum tree
Solid tree-dwelling marsupial. Fluffy and grey. Sleeps a lot.
Can you see him among the gum leaves? Grey/brown/white furry marsupial.
Captured on motion-activated infra-red trail camera at night in a large old growth bush remnant in dry sand country. Individual was walking between trees
Grey furry mammal iconic for Australia spotted snoozing up a tree. Likes eating gum leaves
Cute and cuddly. Grey fur all over. Consumes eucalyptus leaves and sleeps most of the time.
It amazes me the contorted positions these animals will sleep in. They often look like they're dead.Grey fur all over, about 50-60cm long and sharp black claws for climbing trees.
A stocky grey furry marsupial seen high in a eucalyptus tree. Holding on with strong looking claws.
Trying it's best to sleep through the noisy people below
This male was making some fierce noises towards a nearby male. you can see the female he was interested in in the third picture - she's on the left and he's on the right
A pair of koalas looking to mate. The male climbed the wrong tree and was quite confused/frustrated. Then they paused for something to eat and a nap.
A gorgeous Koala just hanging out in a Eucalyptus!
Far away having a sleep in a pine tree. Sorry for the blurred picture.
Up 15m in tree above wetlands. Eating and sleeping
Down one tree, up another in Waite Abortoreum

Grey fur all over except chest area where it is white. About 60-70cm sitting height. Large fluffy ears but small beady eyes. Large claws for climbing and gripping. This specimen was so close I didn't crop the images.
Not the best pics, but there's no mistaking the cute grey furred, big eared, eucalyptus eating lazy bones.
Koala way up a tree. Photo is lightened and adjusted so that it doesn't look like a dark blob. One of three koalas sighted on the island.
Furry grey marsupial. Loves gum trees. Often seen sleeping in eucalyptus branches in positions more like they're dead, like this case.
old mate Bazza seemed  non-perplexed by our presence. Look how close he let me get to him!! I think he's even smiling in one pic
On manna gum inside Michael Perry Reserve

Funny story, we were at Belair National Park for a wedding and as we were leaving I was commenting to my family that it would have been nice if I could have seen a koala in the park. Just as I finish saying that, my sister looks up into the trees as we are driving along and sees one!!! We stop and turn around and are all able to see him. He looked quite happy, scratched himself a few times and watched us. ??
a young doe, photo taken when she left one tree to go to another.
A lone koala besides a walking trail.
Grey, furry, cuddly marsupial. Forever sleeping in positions that appear quite uncomfortable.
screeching alerted us to its presence and eyes in the torchlight identified his location high up in one of next doors gum - pretty sure its a male
A one from last year I think, not much opportunity for exploring with quarantine going on, looking back though my vaults
The female chased the male across the road and and up the tree and then mated.
Found sitting on a fence right next to a main road. Adult with lots of light patches. Black nose. Large ears. Claws for climbing trees  Looked very healthy
Clinging to the branch in strong winds

lucky enough to spot another Koala! This one was smaller than the last one I spotted and I happened to see it when it was a bit active, moving its head around at least. really high up in a tree though so hard to get a good photo.
Large Koala found very close to the River Torrens and not far from the coast. Was quite high up in a gum tree so unable to get a better photo.
two koala sightings on one walk! i think they've come out to see why all the humans are in the forest all of a sudden
Walk last Sunday and only sw one koala, but this one was in a very small tree, strangely it was an Acacia I reckon, but made for an easy capture. Saw two more today, put them in later.
came down the tree and toddled off looking for another one
A female with significant cystitis - sad face

Very lazy koala, not very high up (approx. 3 metres from ground level). Didn’t seem bothered by our presence and began to scratch its butt lazily until we left. Captured: 15/04/2020 at Black Hill Conservation Park, South Australia
Not a very great photo, as they were very high up in the tree on the bad side of the sun. In the trees along the path/road as you walk up to Morialta. There were several amongst the trees.
Raining, every time I got out the car, and the koalas were very high but this one was at least recognisable.
Slept all day, very weary of noise.Must have been moving during the night to a more suitable home and food source.
After-dinner visitor maintaining social distance. Have seen evidence of them being in the yard however this is the first sighting in the yard.
koala at banks street reserve, got some better footage of it but I can only upload photos here
sighted 9th May 2020 while walking on the Waite loop.  It was happy for me to come up close and seemed as interested in me as I was in it.  Was it showing me it's tummy?
This koala nearly climbed up my dad! Walked right in front of him! Sighted at First Trail at Morialta Conservation Park.
birds alerted us to a koala crossing the open back yard and climbing up a mangrove tree by the water
Not one, but TWO koalas spotted within 50 m of each other at the Mt Gravatt Lookout Reserve, Qld.
seen high up in the tree didn't move at all during 15 mins we observed it
A big boy right at the very top of a gum. At least 10 metres off the ground. I've been told a dirty bum is a sign of chlamydia, so I always check. This guy looked clean and healthy.
have heard and seen a few in recent weeks.
I think was about to change trees before I disturbed it - so she (I think) headed back up
In a conservation park in the Adelaide Hills. I never get tired of seeing them.
a large male - grunting in the night, making us aware of his presence
small, probably a female. In a recreation park in the Adelaide Hills.
Healthy male spotted around midnight. No sign of any disease, in habitat dominated by Eucalypts, mainly Tallowwood
Found in eucalyptus trees near the river.

this little female has Cystitis. Koala Care group assisted in capturing her and hopefully she'll be cared back to full health.  Grunting 50 meters away was a large male who was probably disappointed she was taken.
Cute, furry native Australian animal. Eats eucalyptus leaves. Sleeps 20 hours per day.

While we watched it slept for a few minutes before waking and started making a grumpy throaty loud noise, then it fell back asleep. It was only a metre and a half above the ground and right next to the track. It didn't seem to care much about us at all. There was another one a little further down the hill.
Poop on ground in large and small size, suggesting female and Joey. Eating leaves in the crown of the tree. Active while weather overcast.
Medium sized individual in a manna gum in a plantation.
Spotted this cool guy walking on the road after dropping off my kids to school. Parked my car on the kerbside to watch it climb onto a tree.
On the move on a back road, climbed this tree until I’d gone past.
Sitting in a tree by the road. Quite large in size.
Adelaide Hills. The second photo was taken about 30 minutes after the first photo (on the walk back).
A solid marsupial sleeping in a gum tree.
Heard calling up a eucalyptus tree.
Spotted in the wild near Grey River
Chubby, furry grey marsupial with a habit of sleeping in eucalyptus trees.
A hefty furry tree dwelling mammal. Grey and white. This one has cimbed the wrong tree, and looks confused as it searches for food.
Spotted in wild habitat in the Tower Hill reserve. A baby can be seen clinging to its mum clearly in one picture.
Koala asleep high in a ficifolia tree, right in the middle of the campgrond. A hit withall the kids.
This poor guy is struggling in the 46 degree heat. He not only sat in this bucket but drank from the hose. Praying for cooler weather!
Unmoving in a tree as we walked along a path, on the way back it had turned around
This sleepy koala was quite low down in the gum tree. Easily missed by the  numerous passers by who all walked further on to look at the ocean view.
Distinctive Aussie marsupial. Stocky, sleepy, grey fur all over with large fluffy white ears.
In a eucalypt tree at the edge of dry rainforest on Aroona Station. Spotted late afternoon. Seen during the Aroona BugCatch 2019.
Sitting in a tree watching soccer practice

Looking somewhat surprised about being a tourist attraction, or perhaps just at being awake, this handsome and robust individual was having a good look around from the safety of a tree branch just next to a road... admitedly, the road probably isn’t always in heavy use, but in the warmth of summer several visitors had pulled over their cars to catch a glimpse of the iconic local resident. Yes, I supose I might have been one of those tourists! Shocking!
In the same tree as the day before; sleeping this time. On the wdge of the dry rainforest at Aroona Station, Mount Mort, Qld. Spotted mid-morning during the Aroona BugCatch 2019.
Spotted during mid-day. Was fast asleep.
Often to be seen in the park if eyes are cast upward. Saw two today and this image turned out best
Koala found off the Lorikeet track in Belair National Park, another koala was in the tree next door but was hard to photograph
Grey marsupial - 40cm in length. Bunched up between two branches, not moving (resting). Weather - fair wearher 21°C.
A koala sitting on the tree
Best photo  I could get. In manna gums at flinders chase NP
As photos show the hairy boy was relaxing next to the tennis courts.

Single koala seen very high up in a eucalypt tree. Was a very windy day and koala seemed to sway meters at a time but didnt come down any lower so maybe they were having fun. Was quite a small koala presumably a young female. She was stationary for quite a while then became quite active moving up and down the tree and reaching for far leaves and branches. She was a cutie :-)
too high up for better photo unfortunately
This is not a great photo, but I was so excited to see a koala on Mt Coot-tha - the first time I’ve seen one here.
many eucalyptus tree which koala eats theleaves
Two of them in neighbouring trees. One sitting in the fork and the other feeding. Not great photos on dusk but  pretty easy to see what it is.
in strong wind Koala holds on for dear life
Koala Joey on the back of its mother, moving to another tree.

DescriptionThe koala or, inaccurately, koala bear is an arboreal herbivorous marsupial native to Australia. It is the only extant representative of the family Phascolarctidae and its closest living relatives are the wombats, which are members of the family Vombatidae.

I found a koala in its natural habitat in a gum tree. It was eating eucalyptus leaves. It was right at the top of the tree where the new leaves were. I watched the koala choose the tastiest leaves to eat.
Heavy looking specimen, looks like a male.
Cute grey furry Australian icon. About the size of a small dog. Large ears and prominent black nose.
Just outside the binnu burra lodge restaurant. Large koala. Eating before sunset.
A few in this little place in the middle of the big smoke of the Gold Coast
Lounging high in a gum tree
This little koala was sitting in my friend ficus tree on her property. He looked very healthy.
Found walking/hopping on the ground before climbing a tree (which I think is Corymbia intermedia). About 50cm tall/long from head to bottom. White speckling on the lower part of the body.
One koala resting high in the tree in Belair National park right on a walking trail
Taking a nap in a tree. Whats blue and not heavy?Light blue
Koala. uncommon sighting in White Rock Spring Mountain Conservation Estate.
This beauty arrived in our tree overnight and shifted up and down the tree throughout the day before disappearing from sight this afternoon. It appeared to have a blue tag in its left ear.
Hazelwood park. Up a tree asleep
This koala spent some time moving up and down several trees today as if trying to decide which tree it preferred! 😊
Wild mother and joey sighted on the outskirts of dense bushland.

Saw a lot of poo on the ground. Looked around and found one tree had lots of scratches on it so looked up to find the koala. Whilst searching I heard something fall out of the tree and found fresh poo! Koala had a look around and then moved further up the tree.
This pair seen on the Family Tree at redlands near Toondah Harbour
Sighted on The Forts walking track on Magnetic Island
sitting in E Sideriphoia grey ironbark near roadside
Koala sitting in tree just after getting attacked by maggpies
This animal is a de-sexed male. He is a regular visitor that was released in the area by Parks Victoria. You can see his ear tag in the photos.
Mum and bubs making a mad dash across the yard
Resting in gum tree near coast
Tree dwelling mammal. Grey fur all over. Sleeps most of the day. Eats eucalyptus leaves the rest of the day.
sleeping in the rain. single animal. resting
Mum and bub. She hase one every year
Way up high sleeping in fork of tree
On the side of a dirt road. Drove past twice in the last week and he has moved a couple of trees. Very dry out there, hope he'll be okay.
spotted across the highway in a tree on top of a ridge.
We spotted a number (6) koala's from the road to the Cape Otway lighthouse.

In tree next to house. Heard growling during the night then sighted in the day. Hear them every month or so but only spot them about 5 or 6 times a year.

records.notes: Two males separated by 50m. One male had large fresh cut running down the left eye, eye closed
Moving around during day. I heard a male calling the other night

records.locality: Mum and baby seen together in a tree.
Male heard calling from property. A female was also seen sleeping.
In a tree at rear of property. Did not see but could hear the mating cal
Sleeping in a tree at back of house.
records.notes: One koala sighted as part of the National Koala Count Report - http://koalacount.org.au/Community/Sighting/1948849
2 koalas sighted. Koala's are seen occasionally (3-10 times per year). The observer estimates that the animal was a mum and bub. Photo supplied.

records.locality: In a tree in the backyard of 2-4 Hill Crescent, Barhs Scrub
records.notes: He moves around different trees on our property and in the local area, sometimes we don't see him for a week or so but he always comes back. Seen commonly (more than 10 times per year).

records.locality: In a tree in the yard.
records.notes: Male and female pair breeding. Boy chasing girl round my garden for several weeks. Feeding or sleeping when he wasn't chasing her.

records.locality: Heard in trees in Springwood Conservation Park behind 46 - 54 Deloraine Ave Springwood

records.notes: Photo verified sighting. Mum & Bub have been hanging around the general area for about the past month or so. Both very healthy. Two koalas reported as part of the National Koala Count Report - http://koalacount.org.au/Community/Sighting/1973143

records.locality: In a tree next to house.

Thanks to Barbara for the initial sighting of this young Koala. It was in a tree between a station carpark and the rail line. Because of the location it was reported to the local wildlife rescue. Not the best of images as the koala was in a tree with the setting sun directly behind it.
Taken on what I believe was the coldest day on record for Magnetic Island, and this poor little guy was looking pretty freezing!
Spotted in the Eucalypt forest at tidbinbilla
Mating season, calling regularly, in regenerated bluegum plantation. Seen regularly in this area. Has a large selection of eucalypt species nearby.
Young koala.  Seems it may have previously been in a nearby tree that had fallen.  Almost looked too young to be on it's own.
Mum and bub in an acacia. Just off Ewarts. Rd.
Inside the Koala enclosure at TB.
Previously unseen koala, new nose pattern
Female koala (not seen before) resting high in a tree on the western side of McKinnon Drive
One of about six koalas inside the special reserve for them at Tidbinbilla.
No sulking please! :-)  (Part of the enclosure pop. at Tidbinbilla)
New joey, just emerged and acknowledged by rangers this day.

Healthy mature koala;  sitting in the branch of a, presumably of planted origin, spotted gum (Eucalyptus maculata) tree.  (With a Grevillea robusta planted tree in the left foreground) .   Added a cropped image of this koala, from this original first photo .
Older pic from 2017. Single koala spotted in a tree near the road.
To all the mums out there, Happy Mother's Day! :-)
Koala fell out of the tree into the river, swam to shore and then climbed the tree again.
At the Tidbinbilla Koala enclosure. Just putting up some fun photos until some wild pics come in. Kind regards, Roy.

Stzelecki Ranges Koala. Most genetically diverse population in Oz.

my first koala sighting in my local area after 6 years of looking. yay!
Single koala snoozing in a tree

records.notes: 12:05 Midday, walking up the side of the gully, a male koala gave a single call quite close by.
One calling in bushland to south of Breakfast Creek Rd, 10pm

A koala gave a low-pitched growl, from one of the tall eucalypts in Frenchman Creek, if it had not have done so there would have been 0% chance of me even knowing it was there. Spent a long time looking, unable to spot it.  11:30

Coming back up out of Distill creek we noticed extremely high numbers of koala scats on the ground. Then we started scanning the canopy and after a while Bridget spotted a large male koala. We walked a bit closer and it woke up, and climbed even higher in a tall eucalypt. Great views.12:15
Male grunting around 8 AM, probably from a stand of mature eucalypts, mostly manna gums, on the roadside near the bridge.
At 19:00 a male koala called from nearby, but i was unable to see it. This area had a mix of tall trees next to the lerderderg river, and some very small saplings.
20:26After leaving the first site, we drove further down and got out and looked and saw a koala right down in the bottom of the steepest part of the gully.

records.locality: Steiglitz Historic Park. Heard calling, late afternoon along walking track

records.notes: A single male koala beating the heat by resting in a shady blackwood during the day.
Saw on ground before it climbed it's way up young eucalypt, 'grunting' as it went up.  Just after sunrise.
One calling from adjacent bush, Outlook Tk, Brisbane Ranges 8.45 pm
at least this number calling early morning, scattered along track and lake
Walking north, a male koala called from somewhere near the geographic centre of Bamganie State Forest at 21:10
A large, mature male koala was sighted next to Spring Creek Track at 21:33.
A male koala called from somewhere nearby at the junction of Glider and Loop Tracks at 01:24

records.locality: Island Track, Brisbane Ranges National Park
records.notes: A female koala with a very pale rump and lower back and chocolate-brown upper back, in a tree.

One Koala high in Eucalypt. During a survey of area with 4 other GFNC members and Roger Thomas from Ballarat Environment Network. Could not get a photo to submit to iNaturalist and not sure other observers saw this species - so submitted here to make sure the species is recorded for the site!
At 8:30 PM, a male was heard grunting from the roadside near the bridge.
One crossing the Great Ocean Rd, 4 pm.
Two individuals in separate trees on the east side of You Yangs
Adult male firmly wedged between three arterial branches.

records.locality: Geelong-Ballan Road, Brisbane Ranges National Park

records.notes: Small Koala, looks healthy. Dense regrowth post 2006 bushfire. Sitting on a fork in a small tree, hanging on to a larger dead tree.
Sitting low down partially dead tree stump just to the side of the track.
Two seen fairly near each other upstream from the caravan park.
A koala, male, feeding high in a eucalypt, about 12:40. He would pull small bunches of leaves towards him, sniff them and then eat a few.
Grunting loudly for a few seconds from grove of eucalypts. We couldn't find it for a photo. First time I've recorded Koala in Long Forest for many years. I really did want a photo!
At about 21:25 two koalas called, probably males. They were in opposite directions but neither was very far away.
At 12:14, while walking up Saltwater Road, a Koala was spotted high in a Blue Gum.  Looking at the photo zoomed in cannot determine sex.
Active individual seen climbing around in a Mountain Ash.
At 18:05 a male koala called from the northwest, or just after sunset.  Later on a female was observed sitting in the fork of a messmate down to the south east.
Sleeping at the top of a spindly Blue Gum directly above the Bambra-Aireys Inlet Road.
One male koala called several times after dark: 1845, 19:03, 19:46 to the northwest.  One very small, young Koala spotted to the southeast while walking back to the car.
Put the recorder on and left it for a little while-- A male koala can be heard calling at 19:06 and again at 19:47.
While walking 8km around Kangaroo track and the gully below it, heard two male koalas bellow, and spotlit a third  20:40 til 22:30
A koala sighted high in a eucalypt expertly hidden in thick foliage.  Almost impossible to photograph.  13:16.
On roadside with indigenous trees next to paddock. Awake in fork near top of tree
at least 4 individuals calling loudly in various parts of forest around Lake Elizabeth
From the top of Switch road I sat and listened with my recording gear turned all the way up and heard a male Koala call somewhere in Anakie Gorge below me several times after sunset.
A male Koala performed a mating call somewhere below me in the gorge at 21:29
At 20:40, immediately after entering the bottom of the gully, a Koala was observed high an a mature eucalypt.
After walking down to the Ingliston Granites, and not seeing very much at all, I checked Falcons Lookout Track just in case and saw a Koala in a tree beside the track. 22:21.

At 00:28 a plane flew overhead and the noise must have disturbed the Koalas because two called immediately: one to the south-east and one to the northwest.  Interestingly a sugar glider also started to call a few minutes later and then a powerful owl as well.

I don't think I saw two Koalas, instead I think that I scared one so badly it got out of the tree where I first saw it (21:05) and moved quite a distance where I saw it again on the way back up the track (21:53) It had a visible scent patch so must have been a male.

While driving slowly back into Forrest from Lake Elizabeth, my co-pilot spotted three Koalas in trees next to Kaanglang Road, over the length of the entire trip.  We pulled over and got out to take photos of the first two, but the third was in a narrow dangerous part of the road so we kept driving.  Bridget is now five Koalas ahead in our Koala spotting competition

At 12:21 two Koalas were observed in the same tall tree about ten meters away from the Lake Elizabeth toilets. Both were asleep, and one was in a fork low in the tree, the other in a fork high in the tree.
A Koala was observed sitting on a low branch in a Eucalypt in a very humanesque fashion at 22:12 near where the walking track and the Bike Trail diverge.
At 13:08, just after turning onto Orchid Track from Fence Track, we observed a Koala in a short eucalypt off to our left.  Its coat was largely tan, or brown, unlike many koalas.

While walking beside the Barwon at 21:01 a male Koala started calling from somewhere on the opposite side of the river. The Koala did many different calls, its entire repertoire it seems. Lasted quite a few minutes.
While walking through the picnic ground at Meredith Education Area, I noticed I was being observed closely by a very awake and alert Koala in a very tall, straight tree. 13:53.
It appeared to be a male and female in the same tree.
A Koala was perched high in a gum of some sort in the Lerderderg Gorge at the bottom of Link Track Number 2. On our way back to the car it was still in the same place.  10:42 and 16:19.

I had started walking and had to go back to the car and noticed a Koala sitting in the fork of a tree in the Anakie Gorge car park.  It was still present when I returned much later  however it had moved to an even higher branch.  08:15 and 12:45.
At around 16:00, awake and feeding quite low down in small tree in the picnic area. Likely the same animal as Ross saw a few days earlier in same location.
From 19:09, for about an hour, a very talkative male koala performed his various calls in spurts from somewhere down near the creek.
A koala was spotted halfway up the curved trunk of a large Messmate at 20:37 near Spring Creek
Walking along Loop Track, where I have seen Koalas very often before, I noticed one sitting high in a tree. It appeared as though it was enjoying sunning itself in the warm rays of the sun.  14:30.
Parked beside the road and listening through audio equipment, a male Koala was able to be heard calling from somewhere to the south west starting at 22:15.
Single adult feeding in small Eucalypt (sp?), Branding Yards walking track, near Bunjil geoglyph.
A male Koala called from somewhere to the north at about 03:45.  Sounded like the breeding call.

records.locality: Brisbane Ranges, Lower Stony Creek Reservoir
records.notes: Foraging in small eucalypt near wall of reservoir.
Adult in tree by the Moorabool River, below the Belcher property

records.notes: NPR/NGS RADIO EXPEDITIONS Show: Australia Log of DAT 1: labeled A-3 Koala Bellows (Lone Pine Sanctuary, March 11, 2000) Peter Sculthorpe MS Senn Logged by Joan Kelly at Magian Design Studio, Australia Engineer:   Date:  11 March 2000 ng = not good ok = okay g   = good vg = very good Time Description Rating 00:00 Start recording - low level insects in BG and low level hum through most of recording. 00:20 Cockatoo squawk ok 00:30 Scraping sounds and branch breaking 01:06 koala groaning, close in left channel - scraping sounds continue vg 01:35 Koala groans increase in intensity - more textural - to 01:50 Followed by leaves vg 01:55 More distant koala - lost of leafy sounds g 02.20 Short crow calls in MG ok 02:27 Engine in BG - gone by 2:35 02:35 Groaning koala in left channel - becomes vg - birds in BG g 3:12 Other koalas join in BG, and koala in FG stops. Two or three others join in, in MG, left and right channels g 04:00 FG koala joins in, in left channel, MG still in right  vg 04:45 Cockatoo in BG - no koalas.  Distant traffic. ok 5:14 Single soft koala grunt in left channel 5:15 Short crow caws in MG ok 05:25 mournful bird calls g 05:42 Crow again and general twittering General scratching around sounds.  Branch breaking ok 6:25 Koalas start up again in FG in left channel, then both channels Continue until ~7.30 vg 8:04 Rustling leaves, birds in BG g leaves 8:45 Insects become predominant again in right channel ok 09:08 Plane in BG - segment ends 09:30 NEW SEGMENT:  chatter. Previous segment continues. 09:55 Koala groaning gently in right channel - short session. g 10:13 Another takes over in BG - another short session.  Occasional cockatoo in BG and leaf rustles  ok 11:13 Several soft groans in BG in left channel.  **noise in right channel Various birds in BG 12:30 Branch sounds then koalas start up again - until 13:46 Beautiful texture. vg 13:57 Very BG koalas in left channel - then talking ng 14:28 Segment ends 14:45 NEW SEGMENT Alex Chadwick in right.  Peter Sculthorpe in left 10 March 2000, 10.15am Split track, KMR81's 16:00 Interview begins:  Alex interviewing Peter A. Just tell me your name and how we should identify you. P: I'm Peter Skulthorpe, Australian composer A. Were you working here this morning?  When I called you yesterday you said you were working. P: Yes.  This is my studio, and at present I'm working on a film, a documentary film about Australian beach culture.  Its about the hedonism of the beach, the poetry, the painting and the music inspired by the beach, and its got wonderful shots taken all round Australia of Australia's edge.  So that's exciting. A. Who's that for? P. It's for Don Featherstone Productions but its being financed mostly by a Japanese company.  But I think its being shown at a documentary film festival at Cannes on April 10, which is a month from this very day we are doing the interview, so its going to have to be done fairly quickly. A. Is it one of these IMAX films, I know you've done them before. P. No, I haven't done an IMAX.  It's just for TV really.  In fact I don't like doing films very much.  I'm doing this because the director is a very good friend and I enjoy working with friends. A. But you don't like films? P. I like films, but I find that the more people involved in a project the more time it takes, and, frankly, I'd prefer to work between me and my desk.  And also the more people involved in a project the more different opinions there are, and so on, so I'd rather just get on with my own music.  It's different, though, working with a friend.  Because in  the same way if, say, I'm writing a cello piece,  I like to know the player well.  I like to write music for friends and if I know the instrument that's even more exciting.  Therefore, writing film music for a director who's a friend is the same thing really.  Its to do with the hear I think.  Music has to be about the heart. 18:50 A. Let me ask you about the Australian heart.  Is that what you're trying to explore in your music about Australia? P. Yes.  Once upon a time I used to say that -  when people would ask me what kind of a composer I am - I'd say I'm a religious composer, and people would say, Catholic? Methodist?  Anglican?  But, of course, I didn't mean it in the denominational sense.  I meant it in the fact that my music seeks the sacred in the Australian landscape, and the sacred in nature.  And in this way, perhaps, I'm not unrelated to our indigenous people and their approach because in all their art they seek the sacred in nature.  So that's the kind of composer I am, really.  But how does one do it?   I spend quite a bit of time in the Outback, in Central Australia and in Northern Australia (plane in BG - Peter stops for a moment). 20:38 Peter begins again: P. I spend a good deal of time in Central Australia and also in Kakadu and Arnhem Land.  Oddly enough I've never been to Torres Strait, although much of my music has been inspired by Torres Strait music.  That's my next trip I think.  Sometime this year.  But I can't really explain what I do without getting technical in a music sense.  But I can tell you one technique that I use, and that is, just as the Australian landscape is very flat - this is in the centre of Australia - there is very little change, I mean you can go for a walk in the morning and what you see at lunch time is much the same as what you saw when you left.  The sun might have just changed some aspects of it.  Therefore that's always suggested to me that there should be a slow rate of harmonic change.  In other words, the harmonies underlying the music remain for a long time before they change.  That makes writing music difficult because you risk getting very boring, of course.  So I have to find other ways in order to create tension. Sometimes, every now and then on that walk, in the Outback, a big rock will protrude so on the way in the music I can have a sudden rock in the music, if you like, or a sudden flight of birds.  But I have to find ways to keep the music going.  Basically, all of my music has that slow rate of harmonic range. A. But you also have talked in the past, and at times when you talked about joyous music.  Quick, fast music.  Fast joyous music, and that's not.. 22:50 P. Yes.  You can still have joyous music above that slow rate of harmonic change.  In fact, that is my present feeling about my music.  I am very concerned about the growth of world population.  If the population has doubled itself by the middle of this century, I am sure that science will solve the problems of food and energy.  But it's the compounding of human hatred that concerns me.  So then, all my music from now, for the rest of my life, will be trying to pass on a feeling of goodness, of joy, of love.  Because that too can compound itself.  And if others can do this in their work, instead of mirroring what is going on around us, perhaps we can achieve something. (pause for plane in BG) A. Could you tell me what you think it is - what is an Australian? 24:50 P. Oh Alex.  What is an Australian.  Well there's no doubt that we're very easy going.  (interrupted by phone)   A. What is an Australian.  I guess what I want to get at is, I mean you've moved Australian music.  You've told people you've come to think and believe and write and have directed the feelings of others to say that we're not a European country. 26:07 P. It always seemed to me to be perfectly clear that we're not, but many Australians felt, and perhaps still feel, that we should ally ourselves with Europe.  But I've always felt very close to Asia.  I love Asian countries and for me that's what's special about being Australian.  First of all, there is this amazing continent that I love passionately, and there's easy access to Asia.  I think we have a little way to go, we Australians.  We do have to bring about reconciliation with our indigenous people.  It distresses me that Australia was always about the land.  The land was our heart, our soul,  and we've done our best to destroy a lot of it.  But we've also lost our links to it, and I think, therefore, that we could learn from our indigenous people.   Because we are a very easy going lot, we don't take things perhaps as seriously as we should.  But still, that's all right.  But because of that we don't seem to produce great statesmen because we tend not to take politics very seriously, and I think we badly need some visionary politicians.  That to me is one of our great lacks at the moment.  On the other hand, I know of no country - I do travel quite a lot - and I know of no country where there's a better quality of life.  Admittedly I'm biased, being Australian of course, but trying to be objective, that's the way it seems to me. A. When you go out across Australia, you have this kind of - the crescent edge is green and populated, but out in the middle its really...  I remember flying from Perth to Sydney thirty years ago and looking down from the plane and saying, good Lord, this just goes on and on and on and on and there's nothing down there. P. I find that very inspiring in its awesomeness.  But you mentioned the edge of Australia.  In the film that I'm writing the music for, we're told that four out of five Australians live within a short drive from the beach.  Whether that's true or not is an amazing statistic.  It just shows how empty the centre is, really. A. Did you visit the centre of Australia before you began writing about it? 29:44 P. Well that's a very interesting question, because most of my music had been influenced more by Asia than by the outback of Australia, and then finally I came home and began writing music about, particularly the Northern Territory, and I'd never been there.  For instance, I wrote an orchestral work, Kakadu, which was a commission by an American, actually, for first performance at the Aspen Music Festival in 1988.  And I called the piece Kakadu, but I'd never been to Kakadu.  (plane in BG over dialogue) I had books and photos and so on (stop for plane). 31:20 I had books, lots of books, about Kakadu and photographs and so, and I sort of had those all round me and I wrote this piece.  The piece - it's a fairly bold, quite a strong piece, even wild at times.  And then about a year after I'd written it I went to Kakadu and I realised that most of the photographs I had were very dramatic photographs because they made good photographs, and I didn't feel the drama there that was in the books I had.  So, if I'd written Kakadu after I'd been there it would have been a very different piece.  So I'm glad I hadn't been there.  But the music that I wrote about Kakadu, from that point, was much more calm and serene, because when I arrived there I felt very much at home, very happy.  And it wasn't like the original Kakadu piece at all. Afterthought:  Then on the other hand, Vaughan Williams had never been to Antarctica when he wrote the music for Scott of the Antarctic; or Pacini had never been to the golden West and certainly Copland had never been to the West when he wrote his cowboy pieces.  And for that matter, Janicek had never been to the moon, so I don't think it's all together necessary. A. Could I ask you about - is it Nourlangi (chat about pronunciation between Alex and Peter) A. What about that piece? 33:40 P. Well that piece is much less, although it has a little drama, it's much less dramatic that the original Kakadu piece.  It has more serenity in it.  It's also a little bit dramatic too, because when I was writing it I imagine Torres - who sailed for Spain and sailed through Torres Strait, named after him - and when he was sailing through the Strait a guitar fell off the ship and it was lying there resonating in the sea, and when I was writing the guitar music I kept thinking of that and had that sound in my mind, of those lovely resonances.  And again, that was written for the Australian guitarist, John Williams.  Again, I wrote for somebody I know well.  (waiting for plane) A. That piece opens - its seems as though I'm outside and listening to the forest. 35:20 P. Yes, and there's thunder and I think there's a little rain there.  I don't often use or imitate real sounds, except sometimes I use rain sticks, and a thunder sheet, and also bird sounds.  I have violins, or strings, imitating bird sounds.  (plane again - until 36:15).  Just over a year ago I wrote an orchestral piece for a Japanese orchestra, and I went to Japan for the performance, and it had about 12 seconds of thunder sheet and when I arrived at rehearsal, there was the thunder sheet behind the orchestra.  It was bigger than a movie screen!  And I thought, this is really embarrassing for just 12 seconds of music.  So there and then I had to somehow find a way to get more thunder in the piece to make it worthwhile.  But I enjoy things like that. A. That's the piece that I heard and thought - that is so Australian - because its got this wildlife, this sense of landscape.  Its got this openness and these influences that sound Asian to me, picking up in it. P. I should mention that when I made my first visit to Kakadu National Park I climbed up on top of the rock, Nourlangi, this massive rock there, and just stood there.  And in my imagination I imagined that I could hear local music of the Gagadu tribe, that I could hear sounds hanging in the air from early colonial settlement, particularly at Port Essington, that I could hear indigenous music from Torres Strait and even Gamalan music from Indonesia coming in on the wind.  And somehow, all those musics seemed to - I imagined them and they fused in my mind and that was really the beginning of a new style, so that Nourlangi is, in fact, which was inspired by my first visit to Kakadu and that ushered in what became my style during the 90's.  I'm not quite sure where I'm heading at the moment, but I'll take some of that with me anyway.  So, therefore, that's a very good example of the landscape and the sound of the landscape - it wasn't only the music of course, it was thunder, bird sounds, everything seemed to come together. A. Do you know what Australia is becoming?  What is your idea of what Australia is becoming?  This is a country that has gone through an awful lot of changes in the last thirty years, and is now in quite a wrestle with its own soul to establish what its going to be, especially in regards to those first people. P. That's almost too difficult to answer. A. And there's the Republic vote, and all that sort of thing. 39:40 P. We are a Republic at heart.  In a way, it seems to me that becoming a Republic in name is just window dressing.  I just thought it was ridiculous to have a referendum, or have all this nonsense about it when we haven't even sorted out reconciliation with our first people.  That seems, to me, to be the first thing we must do.  I think the next thing we need to do is look at our constitution, before we can think about republic.  We often do things the wrong way round because we are in too much of a hurry.  I think a good example is our national anthem.  A former Prime Minister decided that we should have a new national anthem so we had a competition.  Not one anthem that was sent in for the anthem was any good.  They were appalling.  I remember one, written by a woman, the last verse was,  "Out with the guns boys, ratatatatat  We'll shoot the bloody commie's  And that's the end of that." And that's the kind of standard of lyric that was submitted. So then it was decided to hold a plebitite, and we were given a choice of Waltzing Matilda, Advance Australia Fair, or Song of Australia, which is associated with South Australia - only South Australians seemed to know it, nobody else seemed to.   So that was out.  Everybody felt that Waltzing Matilda, which of course, should be our anthem, but everybody felt it was too undignified - not European enough, really.  So Advance Australia Fair was chosen.  But, of course, Advance Australia Fair is stolen from the melody, God Bless the Prince of Wales. A. You can't have Waltzing Matilda, because there're too many words in there that foreigners can't understand. P. Yes, but there are too many words in Advance Australia Fair, and Australians don't even know them.  We've got words in the Beach film like, chunder, which means vomiting - how do you translate that into Japanese. So the melody for Advance Australia Fair is stolen from the melody for God Bless the Prince of Wales.  The last part of it is identical.  So we jettisoned one Imperial anthem, which is a great melody, and took on another Imperial anthem which is a lesser tune anyway, its Victorian and not particularly good - so we still have an Imperial melody, with words that nobody can remember.  And we did this in our hurry to have a new national anthem, and I think that's the way we've been going about things with the republic.  There's no rush.  We can do little things to help it along, but let it evolve, because most Australians feel that we are a republic. A. You're becoming a much less European looking nation, anyway.  How do the European Australians, the older Australians feel about the changes that are coming with immigrations - so many Asians coming into the country. 44:25 P. This is hard for me to say - it's not hard for me to talk about - because I can't talk with any certainty, but there is a certain amount of resentment from older Australians.  On the other hand, I do feel that there's less racism than in any other country I know.  Certainly there is racism, but it doesn't seem to me to be too pronounced.  I didn't object to the whole Pauline Hanson phenomenon because I think that it was good that she actually caused people to be able to give voice to their feelings of racism.  If these feelings are there they should be let out and spoken about.   It hasn't helped Australia's situation in Asia though, unfortunately.
